corrected_value.title: Catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met genotype moderates the effect of disorganized attachment on social development in young children
corrected_value.authors: Hygen, B. W., Guzey, I. C., Belsky, J., Berg-Nielsen, T. S., Wichstrøm, L.

decisions.quote:
It is important to appreciate that our focus on
COMT
should not be read to imply that only this polymorphism may play a moderating role vis-à-vis the effects of disorganization. Rather, we focused exclusively on this candidate gene because we conceptualized this inquiry from its inception as an attempt to test an intriguing and most original hypothesis and, thereby, conceptually replicate and extend the work of Hygen et al. (
2014
).
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding identify Hygen et al. (2014), 'Catechol-O-methyltransferase Val158Met genotype moderates the effect of disorganized attachment on social development in young children' (DOI: 10.1017/S0954579414000492), as the sole target original study whose COMT x attachment disorganization interaction hypothesis is conceptually replicated.

decisions.quote: We offer a conceptual replication, analyzing data on 560 children (males: 275) drawn from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development. As predicted, competitive model-fitting indicated that disorganized infants carrying Met alleles engage in more positive behavior and less negative behavior than other children at age 5 and 11, with the reverse true of Val/Val homozygotes, seemingly consistent with caregiving-controlling and punitive-controlling styles, respectively, but only in the case of maternal and not teacher reports, thereby confirmating a relationship-specific hypothesis.
decisions.location: Abstract, line 53 (also Results, lines 835-839; Discussion, lines 1424-1433)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding record the replication outcome as 'successful'. Under Codebook Rule 1, the authors state a clear overall positive verdict on their conceptual replication of Hygen et al. (2014): competitive model-fitting across both primary (kindergarten) and secondary sensitivity (Grade 6 and linear/continuous) analyses supported the hypothesized model, with the overall patterning of the data matching all four a-priori predictions (divergent positive and negative behavior between disorganized Met carriers and Val/Val homozygotes, no genetic differences among organized children, and relationship specificity to maternal rather than teacher reports). While the authors note that Hygen et al. (2014) found the interaction for change over time whereas the present study intentionally tested levels of functioning, they explicitly conclude that 'The data from the both the primary and sensitivity analyses fit the Hygen et al. (2014) hypothesis' and that 'reasonably consistent support for the Norwegian hypothesis emerged in both inquiries'.

Both the shipped record and blind coding classify the study as a 'replication'. The paper uses an independent US cohort (560 children from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development) to re-test the published COMT x attachment disorganization interaction reported in a Norwegian cohort by Hygen et al. (2014).
